commentary.bottom_line: Two offline studies that evaluated generative AI output aimed at lower-literacy readers both found that simplification lowered content quality or accuracy, which suggests such evaluation can detect a real performance gap. No study has tested whether developer evaluation of this kind leads to safer products for actual lower-literacy patients.

perspectives.view: Two studies evaluated performance for lower-literacy targets. A Chinese study of 360 texts found C-DISCERN quality fell in all 6 models (Qwen 57.0 to 40.5), and a US benchmark of 67 terms found accuracy fell from 4.56 to 3.99. Both were offline, rater-scored, and indirect for patient outcomes, so certainty is very low.

Hazard studies suggest the failures carry clinical weight. At a 7th-grade level, 20% of simplified radiology reports had potential management changes, and 21% of AI-simplified education materials fully preserved clinical content. Fourth-grade prompts omitted safety information. Under-triage near 100% across all literacy strata in one study suggests that comparing strata alone may miss a uniformly unsafe model.

Studies used different ways to represent lower literacy, including simplification prompts, simulated personas, and real lay users writing their own prompts. One simulation found that aggregate scores concealed variation across personas. Developers may need persona and paraphrase testing in addition to a single simplification prompt, because each method probes a different failure.

Both tests used simulated or target-level text rather than real lower-literacy patients. One test framed prompts for older adults in Chinese. Hazard studies in Turkish and French found lower performance than in English, which suggests literacy and language effects may compound for patients with limited English proficiency.

The sole endorsement is a regulatory discussion paper that describes paraphrase consistency across health literacy levels as a relevant consideration. It does not set a requirement, and no cited source establishes a testing standard or acceptance threshold for lower-literacy performance.

In a randomized study of 300 laypeople, higher education and more LLM experience were associated with better information quality, so patients with less schooling may receive weaker answers. Lower-literacy personas in another study preferred expert-written responses over chatbot responses. Patients may need a route to human-written material when AI output falls short.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested whether developer evaluation for lower-literacy users changes model design or reduces harm, and no evaluation has enrolled actual lower-literacy patients, measured their comprehension and actions, or compared evaluation methods such as persona testing, paraphrase testing, and simplification prompts.
commentary.underserved_note: Both tests targeted low health literacy, and one also framed prompts for older adults in Chinese, but neither involved real patients, Medicaid enrollees, or safety-net settings. The findings therefore rest on expert-rated text and may not reflect how lower-literacy patients in underserved settings phrase questions or act on answers.
